title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX & FLEX-2)
principal_investigator: Dr. Forman A. Williams / Dr. Vedha Nayagam
institution: University of California, San Diego / NASA Glenn Research Center
description: The Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) analyzed the burning and extinction characteristics of isolated spherical fuel droplets in microgravity within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the ISS. Droplets of n-heptane, n-decane, and methanol/water mixtures were suspended and ignited. The experiment resulted in the historic discovery of microgravity quasi-steady 'cool flames'—a low-temperature, invisible combustion regime continuing after hot flame extinction.
objectives: Determine the limiting oxygen concentration (LOC) for flame extinction; study radiant extinction vs kinetic extinction limits; examine the influence of inert diluents (CO2, He, N2) on burning rates; observe quasi-steady cool-flame phenomena without buoyancy-driven convection.
fuel_types: n-Heptane, n-Decane, Methanol, Ethanol-water mixtures (Droplets 1.5 - 5.0 mm initial diameter)
oxidizer_environment: O2 in N2, CO2, and He diluents; ambient pressure 0.5 to 3.0 atm; O2 mole fraction 0.15 to 0.40
measured_parameters: Droplet diameter squared decay rate (K in mm2/s), hot flame extinction diameter, cool flame initiation delay, cool flame extinction diameter, radiant emission spectrum.
key_findings: Identified low-temperature chemical kinetics (temperatures 600-800 K) maintaining quasi-steady droplet burning for up to 30 seconds after the hot visible flame self-extinguished due to radiative cooling. Demonstrated that conventional extinction criteria fail to detect ongoing low-temperature oxidation in microgravity.
fire_safety_relevance: FLEX reported continued low-temperature burning in some large n-alkane droplets after the visible hot flame underwent radiative extinction. This result is limited to the tested conditions. The investigation did not establish spacecraft sensor performance or operational risks associated with ventilation restart.

publications.title: Can cool flames support quasi-steady alkane droplet burning?
publications.authors: Nayagam, V., Dietrich, D. L., Ferkul, P. V., Hicks, M. C., Williams, F. A.
publications.journal_or_conference: Combustion and Flame, Vol. 159, Iss. 12, pp. 3583-3588

publications.title: Cool-flame extinction during n-alkane droplet combustion in microgravity
publications.authors: Nayagam, V., Dietrich, D. L., Hicks, M. C., Williams, F. A.
publications.journal_or_conference: Spring Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of the Combustion Institute

findings.finding_text: Sustained cool flame combustion discovered in n-heptane droplets between 1.5 and 5.0 mm diameter at atmospheric pressures in microgravity.
findings.spacecraft_fire_safety_implication: Thermal sensors and optical detectors calibrated for hot flames cannot identify microgravity cool flames, requiring multi-sensor gas analysis (CO/CO2/VOC ratio).
findings.source_citation: Nayagam et al., Combustion and Flame (2012)

findings.finding_text: Droplet burning rate constant K decreases substantially in microgravity compared to normal gravity due to the absence of buoyant convective heat transfer.
findings.spacecraft_fire_safety_implication: Liquid fuel spills burn slower per unit surface area in quiescent microgravity, but unburned fuel vapors accumulate in a spherical cloud around the ignition point.

datapoints.phenomenon: Hot flame followed by second-stage cool flame extinction
Quasi-steady spherical burning with radiative extinction
Near-limit extinction without cool flame formation

title: Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire I - VI)
principal_investigator: Dr. David L. Urban / Gary A. Ruff
facility: Orbital ATK / Northrop Grumman Cygnus Spacecraft (Post-ISS departure)
flight_mission: Cygnus OA-6 (Saffire-I), OA-5 (Saffire-II), OA-7 (Saffire-III), NG-13/14/19 (Saffire IV-VI)
description: The Saffire experiments represent NASA's first large-scale fire safety tests conducted in real microgravity inside an uncrewed Cygnus resupply vehicle after departing the ISS and prior to atmospheric reentry. Saffire evaluated flame spread over large cotton-fiberglass blend fabric (SIBAL) samples (0.4 m wide x 1.0 m long), PMMA slabs, and Nomex materials under realistic spacecraft atmospheric conditions, variable airflow velocities, and reduced pressures.
objectives: Assess realistic large-scale spacecraft fire growth; determine flame spread rates under low-speed ventilation flows (0 to 30 cm/s); validate NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 terrestrial upward flammability screening against microgravity reality; measure toxic off-gas yields (CO, CO2, HCN, soot) and test fire suppression depressurization.
fuel_types: SIBAL (75% cotton / 25% fiberglass fabric), PMMA (polymethyl methacrylate) sheets, Nomex HT90-40, Silicone, printed circuit board substrates
oxidizer_environment: O2 concentrations from 20.9% down to 15.0% and enriched up to 34%; pressures 0.55 atm to 1.0 atm
gravity_environment: Microgravity (~10^-5 to 10^-4 g in Cygnus drift)
measured_parameters: Concurrent and opposed flame spread rate (mm/s), pyrolyzed area (cm2), radiometer heat flux (kW/m2), CO and CO2 concentration (ppm), smoke particle diameter and obscuration.
key_findings: Demonstrated that low-speed forced airflow (typical of ISS cabin circulation, ~10-20 cm/s) actively sustains and propagates flames across materials that self-extinguish in quiescent air. NASA-STD-6001 ground testing was found to be non-conservative in some low-flow microgravity conditions because convective cooling that protects samples in 1g is absent in space.
fire_safety_relevance: Saffire measured flame behavior in specified spacecraft-like test configurations with imposed airflow. The results show that flow and test geometry matter; the cited records do not establish fan-cutoff or depressurization procedures.

publications.title: Results of Large-Scale Spacecraft Flammability Tests
Fire Safety Implications of Preliminary Results from Saffire IV and V Experiments on Large Scale Spacecraft Fires

findings.finding_text: Concurrent flame spread rate over SIBAL fabric in 21% O2 at 20 cm/s flow reached ~1.8 mm/s, while opposed flame spread was limited to ~0.4 mm/s.
findings.spacecraft_fire_safety_implication: Cabin ventilation flow direction directly dictates flame propagation velocity. Emergency fire response procedures must automatically shut down cabin air handling to starve concurrent flame spread.
findings.source_citation: Olson et al., Combustion and Flame (2019)

findings.finding_text: Materials tested under reduced pressure (8.2 psi) and elevated oxygen (34% O2)—the planned Exploration Atmosphere for Artemis lunar missions—exhibited higher flammability than at sea-level cabin atmospheres.
findings.spacecraft_fire_safety_implication: Artemis and Lunar Gateway exploration atmospheres increase flame spread and decrease ignition energy requirements, requiring stricter material screening standards than Apollo or ISS standards.
findings.source_citation: Urban et al., Saffire IV-VI Preliminary Evaluation, NASA ICES (2022)

datapoints.phenomenon: Concurrent forced-flow flame spread along cotton face
Exploration atmosphere enhanced pyrolysis and charring

title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE)
principal_investigator: Dr. David L. Urban / Dr. Peter B. Sunderland
institution: NASA Glenn Research Center / University of Maryland
description: SPICE investigated soot emission limits (smoke points) and flame lengths in laminar gas-jet diffusion flames in microgravity. Gaseous hydrocarbon fuels (methane, ethylene, propane, and fuel blends) were burned in co-flowing air at varying velocities. Without buoyancy to accelerate exhaust gases, fuel residence times increase dramatically in microgravity, fundamentally altering soot formation, agglomeration, and radiation.
objectives: Determine laminar smoke-point fuel flow rates in microgravity; quantify soot volume fractions and radiative emissions; observe whether microgravity flames emit smoke at lower fuel flow rates than normal-gravity flames.
oxidizer_environment: Air (21% O2 in N2), ambient ISS cabin pressure (~1.0 atm), co-flow velocities 5 to 40 cm/s
measured_parameters: Laminar smoke point fuel flow rate (SCCM), flame tip soot release, flame length (mm), flame color and luminosity.
key_findings: Discovered that smoke points occur at significantly lower fuel flow rates in microgravity than in 1g (frequently by a factor of 2 or more). Soot remains inside the flame zone much longer due to absence of buoyant updraft, leading to extensive soot aggregation and intense thermal radiation.
fire_safety_relevance: SPICE measured soot-onset and smoke-point behavior in controlled gas-jet diffusion flames under microgravity co-flow conditions. The cited work does not test spacecraft smoke-detector or filtration performance, or ignition of adjacent equipment.

publications.title: Laminar smoke points of coflowing flames in microgravity
publications.authors: Dotson, K. T., Sunderland, P. B., Yuan, Z.-G., Urban, D. L.
publications.journal_or_conference: Fire Safety Journal, Vol. 46, Iss. 8, pp. 550-555
publications.abstract: Laminar smoke points were measured in nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in coflowing air aboard the International Space Station. The study reports 55 smoke points for ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen mixtures.

findings.finding_text: Laminar smoke-point flow rates are reduced by 40% to 60% in microgravity relative to 1g for ethylene and propane diffusion flames.
findings.spacecraft_fire_safety_implication: Microgravity flames soot profusely at lower energy release rates, meaning severe smoke generation starts almost immediately after ignition in spacecraft.
findings.source_citation: Sunderland et al., Combustion and Flame (2011)

datapoints.phenomenon: Early smoke emission due to prolonged microgravity residence time
High radiative soot cooling causing premature tip opening

title: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS & BASS-II)
principal_investigator: Dr. Sandra L. Olson / Dr. Paul V. Ferketic
description: BASS investigated the combustion and extinction characteristics of various solid polymeric materials (PMMA rods, flat slabs, cellulose, cotton fabric blends) in the Microgravity Science Glovebox. Gaseous nitrogen was injected to determine the minimum flow velocity and minimum oxygen concentration required for fire extinction.
objectives: Determine Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) in microgravity with forced concurrent and opposed airflow; evaluate gaseous N2 extinguisher effectiveness; map the extinction boundary curves as a function of flow velocity.
fuel_types: PMMA (rods and flat slabs), Delrin (polyoxymethylene / POM), Cotton/fiberglass fabrics, nomex blends
oxidizer_environment: O2 concentrations 13% to 21%; ambient pressure 1.0 atm; airflow speeds 1.0 to 40.0 cm/s
measured_parameters: Opposed and concurrent burning rates, flame length, extinction velocity, nitrogen suppression concentration, minimum oxygen concentration (MOC).
key_findings: Demonstrated that low air velocities (around 1 to 5 cm/s) produce the most difficult-to-extinguish flames. At higher air speeds, convective cooling can blow the flame out; in perfectly still air, radiation self-extinguishes the flame. However, weak forced flows matching spacecraft air conditioning provide the exact sweet spot for maximum persistence.
fire_safety_relevance: In reported BASS tests, local application of a nitrogen suppressant jet did not extinguish all flame regions in a tested configuration and could entrain surrounding air. This result is configuration-specific; the cited records do not establish general procedures or CO₂ performance.

publications.title: Burning and Suppression of Solids–II (BASS–II) Summary Report
publications.authors: Olson, S. L., Ferkul, P. V., Bhattacharjee, S., Miller, F. J., Fernandez-Pello, C., Link, S., T'ien, J. S., Wichman, I.

publications.title: ISS Results Solid Fuel Combustion-Material Flammability

findings.finding_text: Flames on PMMA slabs exhibit maximum persistence at low flow velocities between 2.5 and 5.0 cm/s, requiring significantly higher nitrogen inerting concentrations than in 1g.
findings.spacecraft_fire_safety_implication: Spacecraft ventilation creates localized micro-drafts (2-5 cm/s) behind panels and racks that maximize solid combustion survivability, creating hidden persistent fire pockets.

datapoints.phenomenon: Near-limit stable flame sustained at low ventilation
Blue non-luminous flame near extinction limit

title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME)
principal_investigator: Dr. Dennis P. Stocker / Dr. Richard Axelbaum
institution: NASA Glenn Research Center / Washington University in St. Louis
description: ACME was a modular suite of six distinct microgravity gaseous combustion experiments hosted in the CIR on the ISS: Burning Rate Emulator (BRE), Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame), Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD), Flame Design, and Structure and Extinction Limit of Strained Diffusion Flames (s-Flame). The experiments investigated soot-free combustion, electric field flame manipulation, and flame extinction limits without buoyancy distortion.
objectives: Determine fundamental flammability and extinction limits for gaseous fuels; understand how electric fields can alter flame stability and extinguish fires without chemical suppressants; assess gaseous burner safety for space habitat propulsion and life-support regenerators.
fuel_types: Methane, Ethylene, Acetylene, Propane, Hydrogen, Carbon monoxide mixtures
oxidizer_environment: O2 in N2, He, Ar, and CO2 diluents; O2 mole fraction 0.15 to 0.50; pressure 0.5 to 3.0 atm
measured_parameters: Radiative heat flux, flame extinction strain rate, ion current under applied voltage (kV), soot volume fraction, flame standoff distance.
key_findings: Demonstrated that moderate DC and AC electric fields can deflect, stabilize, or actively extinguish microgravity diffusion flames by exerting forces on naturally occurring chemi-ions. Showed that radiative heat loss causes abrupt flammability shutoff at low strain rates where 1g flames remain viable.
fire_safety_relevance: NASA’s E-FIELD Flames study measured electric-field effects on selected laminar flames in microgravity. Applying this effect to spacecraft fire steering or suppression remains a hypothesis; the cited study did not demonstrate an avionics-bay suppression system.

publications.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) on the International Space Station (ISS)
Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames)

findings.finding_text: Applied electric fields (0 to 10 kV) exert sufficient body forces on flame chemi-ions in microgravity to induce ionic wind, modifying flame shape and extinguishing diffusion flames at high field strengths.
findings.spacecraft_fire_safety_implication: Provides proof of concept for solid-state electromagnetic fire containment in enclosed electronic chasses in spacecraft without adding consumables weight.

datapoints.source_reference: ACME s-Flame Test Matrix CIR Run 55

datapoints.phenomenon: E-Field destabilization and ionic wind blowout
